questions.title: The ball bounces out
questions.question: The flag has been taken out of the hole. Your ball falls in, then bounces out onto the green. What should you do?

choices.text: Hit your next shot from where the ball stopped.
Count the hole as finished.
Play your last shot again, with no penalty.
Add one penalty shot before you play on.

questions.explanation: The ball must stay in the hole to finish this hole. It bounced out, so keep playing from where it stopped. You do not get a penalty for the bounce.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The ball has finished the hole. Usually it must stay in the hole with every part below the green’s surface. A ball resting against the flagstick has a special rule.

questions.title: Which places are in the general area?
questions.question: Golf calls most of the course the “general area”. Which of these places belong to it? Choose all the correct answers.

choices.text: The rough, where the grass is longer.
The putting green for a different hole.
A bunker, filled with sand.
The putting green for the hole you are playing.
The fairway, where the grass is cut short.

questions.explanation: The fairway, rough and other holes’ greens are in the general area. Your own hole’s starting area and green are not. Neither are bunkers or penalty areas, usually marked red or yellow. You must not play from another hole’s green. Ask an adult to help you move the ball under the rules.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Most of the course, including fairways and rough. It leaves out bunkers, penalty areas, and the starting area and green for the hole you are playing.
A putting green for another hole. You must move clear under the rules if it affects your ball, feet or swing.

questions.teachingTip: Read the situation together. Ask the learner to explain which facts support the correct answer, using the explanation and words explained.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “A bunker, filled with sand.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: The general area

choices.text: The rough.

questions.explanation: The general area includes fairways, rough and other holes’ teeing areas and putting greens. questions.title: One club too many
questions.question: You may carry up to 14 clubs. You find 15 in your bag after starting your round. What must you do before your next shot?

choices.text: Try every club before choosing which one to stop using.
Keep using all 15 and add one penalty shot each hole.
Tell another player which club you will stop using, then leave it unused.
Keep all 15 ready to use until you finish the round.

questions.explanation: Before your next shot, make clear which club you will stop using. Do not use it again this round. You still get a penalty for carrying too many clubs. Ask the scorer to help count it. Playing another shot before taking a club out means your competition score cannot count.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The set of holes you are meant to play, in order. It may be 18 holes or fewer.

questions.title: Finding an extra club

questions.title: Will the ball fall into the hole?
questions.question: Your putt stops with part of the ball hanging over the edge of the hole. How long may you wait for it to fall in?

choices.text: As long as you want.
Only until another player is ready.
Enough time to walk to the hole normally, then ten more seconds.
Only ten seconds from when it reaches the hole.

questions.explanation: Walk to the hole without wasting time. You then have ten more seconds to wait. If it falls in during that time, your putt finished the hole. If it falls in later, before you hit it again, add one penalty shot.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The ball has finished the hole. Usually it must stay in the hole with every part below the green’s surface. A ball resting against the flagstick has a special rule.

questions.teachingTip: Read the situation together. Ask the learner to explain which facts support the correct answer, using the explanation and words explained.

If the learner chooses “Only until another player is ready.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Only ten seconds from when it reaches the hole.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Waiting for an overhanging ball
questions.question: Part of your ball overhangs the edge of the hole after a putt. How long may you wait to see whether it falls in?

choices.text: As long as you like.
Only until another player is ready.
A reasonable time to reach the hole, then ten more seconds.
Ten seconds starting as soon as the ball reaches the hole.

questions.explanation: Allow a reasonable time to reach the hole, plus ten seconds. If the ball falls in within that time, the previous stroke holed it. If it falls in after that waiting time but before you play it, add one penalty stroke.

questions.title: A ball stuck in its dent on the green
questions.question: Your ball lands on the green and makes a dent. It stays stuck in that dent. You want to pick up the ball and fix the dent. What should you do?

Mark its spot, pick it up, fix the dent and put it back on that spot.
Pick it up, then drop it beside the dent.
Fix the dent and put the ball closer to the hole.

questions.explanation: Mark the ball’s spot before picking it up. Repair the dent carefully. Put the ball back on its old spot and take the marker away before putting. There is no penalty.

questions.title: A ball embedded on the green

questions.title: Playing after a drop rolls too far
questions.question: You are counting all your shots in stroke play. You drop the ball correctly, but it rolls outside the allowed drop area. You hit it from there. That spot gives no big advantage. What penalty do you get?

choices.text: None, because you dropped from knee height.
Your score cannot count in the competition.
Two penalty shots.
One penalty shot.

questions.explanation: Add two penalty shots for playing from the wrong place. Here, you keep playing with that score. Before hitting, you should have fixed the drop. Playing from a wrong place that gives a big advantage has extra rules: ask an official for help.

The measured space where a rule lets you drop. The ball must land and stop in the allowed space. Ask an adult to help measure it.

questions.title: Your ball is on the clubhouse patio
questions.question: Your ball is on the clubhouse’s paved patio, inside the course boundary. The rules allow a free drop away from it. You choose that drop. Where must you drop?

choices.text: Anywhere within two club-lengths of your ball.
Inside the measured one-club-length area, fully clear of the patio and no closer to the hole.
Exactly on the nearest spot, even if your feet are still on the patio.
On the nearest fairway spot, even if it is closer to the hole.

questions.explanation: Find the nearest spot where the patio no longer affects your ball, feet or swing. It must not be closer to the hole. Measure one club-length from there. Drop within that area, still fully clear, no closer to the hole, outside bunkers, penalty areas and this hole’s green. Ask an adult to help.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: An object made by people that cannot easily be moved without damage, such as a concrete path. Boundary fences and objects made part of the course’s challenge are different.
The closest allowed spot to your ball where the problem is fully out of the way. It must not be closer to the hole. Ask an adult to help find it.
The length of your longest club for this round, apart from your putter. Use this length to measure where a drop is allowed.
The measured space where a rule lets you drop. The ball must land and stop in the allowed space. Ask an adult to help measure it.

questions.title: Free relief from the clubhouse patio

choices.text: Anywhere within two club-lengths of the ball.
Within one club-length of the nearest point of complete relief, in the general area, not nearer the hole and with complete relief.
Exactly on the nearest point, even if the patio still interferes with your stance.
On the nearest fairway spot, even if that is closer to the hole.

questions.explanation: Complete relief covers the ball’s lie, your intended stance and swing. The reference point may be in rough, but the relief area may also include legal fairway spots. You need not stand inside the relief area while dropping. Relief is optional and does not guarantee a better lie.

questions.title: An extra club you never used

One penalty shot.

questions.title: Fifteen clubs from the start

One penalty stroke.

questions.explanation: Yes. A sensible shot can count even if you would use your other hand. Work out the free-drop area using that left-handed shot. You cannot invent an unreasonable shot just to get a free drop. Ask an adult to help measure.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Moving your ball in a way the rules allow, with no penalty shot for that move. The new spot might still be hard to play from.
An object made by people, such as a path or bench. Boundary markers and objects made part of the course’s challenge have different rules.
How you place your feet and body to hit a shot.

questions.teachingTip: In a practice area, show a blocked right-handed shot and a sensible left-handed shot. Work out relief using the left-handed shot only when that shot is reasonable. Do not invent an awkward stance just to get a free drop.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “No, because you usually play right-handed.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “No. Changing hands can never allow a free drop.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Only if all your clubs are left-handed.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Relief from Cart Path for a Left-Handed Stance
questions.question: A right-handed player's ball comes to rest in the general area beside a tree, blocking any reasonable right-handed stroke. The player could reasonably play the ball left-handed. In taking a left-handed stance, their feet are on an artificially surfaced cart path. Is the player entitled to free relief from the cart path?

choices.text: Yes, provided the left-handed stroke is reasonable in the circumstances.
No, free relief is not allowed because the player is right-handed.
No, changing to a left-handed stroke can never qualify for relief.
Yes, but only if their clubs are designed for left-handed play.

questions.explanation: Yes. Use the reasonable left-handed stroke to find the nearest point of complete relief. Drop within one club-length of that point in the general area, no nearer the hole, with complete relief from the path. From the new lie you may choose a right-handed stroke if it is now reasonable.

questions.title: Bumping your ball before a fairway shot
questions.question: Your ball is on the fairway. Before starting your backswing, your club accidentally bumps it to a new spot. You are not looking for the ball or taking an allowed drop. What should you do?

choices.text: Add one penalty shot and put the ball back.
Play from the new spot, with no penalty.
Put it back, with no penalty.
Add two penalty shots and put it back.

questions.explanation: Add one penalty shot and put the ball back where it was. You moved your own ball before starting the shot. Estimate its old spot carefully if needed. A ball accidentally moved while searching or on the green has different rules.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Getting ready to hit the ball. The rules look at what you actually do, such as starting your backswing.
Most of the course, including fairways and rough. It leaves out bunkers, penalty areas, and the starting area and green for the hole you are playing.

questions.teachingTip: In a practice area, show a club accidentally moving a resting fairway ball. Practise replacing it and count the one penalty stroke. Compare wind moving an unlifted ball, which has a different Rule.

questions.title: Accidentally Moving Your Ball While Addressing It in the General Area

choices.text: Add one penalty stroke and replace the ball.
Play the ball from its new position without penalty.
Replace the ball without penalty.
Add two penalty strokes and replace the ball.

questions.explanation: Add one penalty stroke and put the ball back on its original spot, estimating that spot if necessary. This scenario is in the general area and none of the exceptions for search, the putting green or applying a relief rule applies.

questions.title: Putting a tee down to show where to aim
questions.question: You cannot see the place you want to hit towards. You put a tee in the ground and let go of it to show your aiming direction. Is that allowed?

choices.text: No.
Yes, if you remove it before the shot.
Yes, if you never touch it again.
Yes, if the other players agree.

questions.explanation: No. You must not set an object down to show your aiming direction in this way. Taking it away before the shot does not undo that mistake. Use a feature already there, such as a distant tree, to help choose your direction.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The path you want your ball to take, including the space above and beside it.
A shot where you cannot see the place you want the ball to land.

questions.teachingTip: Show children how to choose a target or spot to aim without putting anything down on the ground.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Yes, if you remove it before the shot.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Deliberately Setting Down an Object to Indicate Line of Play
questions.question: Before a blind shot, may you put a tee on the ground and let go of it specifically to show where to aim?

choices.text: No, the rules do not allow this and a penalty applies.
Yes, as long as it is removed before you play your shot.
Yes, but only if you do not touch the object again.
Yes, if another player agrees.

questions.explanation: Setting down and releasing an object to help aim is prohibited. Picking it up before the stroke does not avoid the general penalty. Choosing an existing landmark is different from placing an aiming object.

questions.title: Putting spare clubs down in a bunker
questions.question: Your ball is in a bunker. You lay spare clubs on the sand away from it. You are not testing the sand or changing anything that could help your shot. Is putting the clubs down allowed?

choices.text: Yes, with no penalty.
No. Clubs must never touch bunker sand.
Only your helper may do it.
Only if your ball is on the green.

questions.explanation: Yes. You may put spare clubs down like this. Your club must not touch bunker sand during a practice swing or your shot’s backswing. It must not touch sand right in front of or behind your ball either. Do not use the spare clubs to test or improve the sand.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A specially prepared area of sand. A grassy bank beside or inside its edge is not itself part of the bunker.
A rule may add extra shots to your score or make you lose a hole. Some penalties mean your result cannot count in the competition.

questions.teachingTip: In a practice bunker, show spare clubs laid down away from the ball. Do not test the sand or improve the ball’s lie, intended stance, swing area or line of play.

questions.title: Placing Clubs in a Bunker
questions.question: Your ball is in a bunker. May you lay spare clubs on the sand away from the ball, without testing the sand or improving the conditions for your stroke?

No, placing clubs in a bunker is not allowed and incurs a penalty.
Only your caddie may place clubs in the bunker, not the player.
You can only place clubs in the bunker if the ball is already on the green.

questions.explanation: Laying spare clubs on sand is permitted in these circumstances. This permission does not allow testing the sand or improving conditions affecting the stroke.

questions.title: Can you repair a club broken in anger?
questions.question: You hit your driver against the ground in anger and break it. May you repair it during this round?

choices.text: No.
Yes.
Yes, but only to make it look better.
No, but you may bring in a different driver to replace it.

questions.explanation: No. The damaged-club rule does not allow repair or replacement when you caused the damage in anger. You can use another club already allowed in your bag. Ask an adult to check the broken club. Do not use it if it could hurt someone.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A club often used for long shots from the tee.
Fix something that is damaged or broken.

questions.teachingTip: Remind children to always respect their clubs and try to keep calm, even when they feel upset.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Yes.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Damaging a club in anger – can you repair it?
questions.question: If you damage your adjustable driver by slamming it on the ground in frustration, may you repair it during the round?

choices.text: No, you may not repair it.
Yes, you may repair it.
Yes, but only for cosmetic damage.
No, but you may bring in a replacement driver from outside your playing set.

questions.explanation: Damage caused by abuse is excluded from the permission to repair or replace a club during the round under Rule 4.1a(2). The player may use other clubs already carried and may continue with the damaged club, but should not use equipment that is unsafe.

questions.title: Your ball makes a dent in the green
questions.question: Your ball lands on the green and sticks in the dent it made. You want to pick up the ball and fix the dent. What should you do?

choices.text: Mark the spot, lift and clean the ball, fix the dent, then put the ball back.
Hit the ball without fixing the dent.
Mark and clean the ball, but the rules do not let you fix the dent.
Drop the ball as close to the dent as you can.

questions.explanation: Mark the spot before lifting the ball. You may clean it and fix the dent. Put the ball back on that same spot, then remove the marker before playing. This kind of dent is called a pitch-mark. Not every bump or worn patch on a green may be fixed.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The area around the hole prepared for putting. It may be flat or sloping.
A dent made when a ball lands on the ground.
Show the ball’s spot with a coin or tee right beside or behind it. You may also hold a club on the ground right beside or behind it.

questions.teachingTip: Use an existing pitch-mark to practise careful repair and marking the ball’s spot. Do not create new damage for the demonstration.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Hit the ball without fixing the dent.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Mark and clean the ball, but the rules do not let you fix the dent.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: What happens if a ball embeds in its own pitch-mark on the putting green?
questions.question: Your ball is embedded in its own pitch-mark on the putting green. You choose to lift it and repair the mark. What is the correct procedure?

choices.text: You may mark and lift the ball, clean it, repair the pitch-mark, and replace the ball on its original spot.
You must play the ball as it lies without repairing the pitch-mark.
You may mark, lift and clean the ball, but must not repair the pitch-mark before replacing the ball.
You must drop the ball as near as possible to where it lay, without penalty.

questions.explanation: On the putting green, mark the spot before lifting. You may clean the ball and repair its pitch-mark with reasonable actions. Replace the ball on its original spot and remove the marker before playing. This permission covers the pitch-mark; it does not allow repairing every kind of wear or natural unevenness.

questions.title: Checking whether your ball made a dent
questions.question: Your ball lands on the fairway. You have a good reason to think it is stuck in its own dent. You need to lift it to check for a free drop, and choose to check. What should you do first?

Hit it without checking.
Lift and clean it before checking.
Say it is stuck without checking.

questions.explanation: Mark the spot and lift the ball. Do not clean it while checking. If a free drop is not allowed, or you choose not to take it, put the ball back. If you take an allowed drop, you may then clean the ball or use another one.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Your ball is in the dent it made when it landed after your last shot. Part is below ground level, not just below the tops of the grass.
Most of the course, including fairways and rough. It leaves out bunkers, penalty areas, and the starting area and green for the hole you are playing.
A small object made by people, such as a coin or tee. Put it right beside or behind your ball to show its spot.

questions.teachingTip: Use a spare ball off the course to show ground level and a pitch-mark. Having a dirty ball alone is not a reason to lift it for this check.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Hit it without checking.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Lift and clean it before checking.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Say it is stuck without checking.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Checking Whether a Ball Is Embedded
questions.question: You reasonably believe your ball is embedded in its own pitch-mark in the general area, but must lift it to check. You choose to check whether free relief is available. What is the correct procedure?

choices.text: Mark the spot, then lift without cleaning to check whether relief is allowed.
Play the ball as it lies without checking.
Lift the ball and clean it before checking if it is embedded.
Declare the ball embedded without lifting or marking it.

questions.explanation: When there is reasonable belief and lifting is necessary to check entitlement to relief, mark the spot and lift without cleaning. questions.title: Taking a free drop from your ball’s dent
questions.question: Your ball is stuck in its own dent on the fairway. A free drop is allowed. The spot just behind the ball is also on the fairway. You choose the drop. What should you do?

choices.text: Measure one club-length from just behind the ball. Drop from knee height into the allowed space.
Clean the ball and put it back in its dent.
Drop from shoulder height within two club-lengths.
Put the ball down within six inches of its dent.

questions.explanation: Start measuring at the spot just behind the ball, away from the hole. The drop area is within one club-length and no closer to the hole than that spot. Keep the drop in the main playing area, outside bunkers, penalty areas and this hole’s green. The ball must land and stop in that space. Ask an adult to help measure.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Your ball is in the dent it made when it landed after your last shot. Part is below ground level, not just below the tops of the grass.
A small object made by people, such as a coin or tee. Put it right beside or behind your ball to show its spot.
The length of your longest club for this round, apart from your putter. Use this length to measure where a drop is allowed.

questions.teachingTip: In a practice area, measure from the point directly behind an embedded ball. A tee or coin can help remember the point but is not compulsory. Drop from knee height into the measured area, no closer to the hole.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Clean the ball and put it back in its dent.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Drop from shoulder height within two club-lengths.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Put the ball down within six inches of its dent.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Taking Free Relief from an Embedded Ball

choices.text: Use the spot directly behind the ball as the reference point. Drop from knee height in the one-club-length relief area, in the general area and no nearer the hole; the ball must also stop in that area.
Remove the embedded ball, clean it, and place it exactly where it was embedded.
Drop a ball from shoulder height anywhere within two club-lengths of the embedded spot, no nearer the hole.
Mark the embedded spot, then place the ball within six inches of that spot, no closer to the hole.

questions.explanation: The reference point is the spot in the general area directly behind the embedded ball. Marking that point is helpful but not compulsory. The original ball or another ball must be dropped correctly and come to rest in the relief area.

questions.title: A ball stuck in sand among long grass
questions.question: Your ball lands and sticks in its own dent in sand among long grass. This is outside bunkers and penalty areas. The grass is not cut short like the fairway. No special course rule allows a free drop. Does the stuck-ball rule give a free drop here?

choices.text: No, because of the sand in this area of long grass.
Yes, every ball stuck in sand gets a free drop.
Yes, only sand in a bunker stops a free drop.
No, a ball stuck in its own dent never gets a free drop anywhere.

questions.explanation: No. This sand is in an area where the grass is longer than fairway grass. The usual free-drop rule for a ball stuck in its own dent does not apply there. Ask an adult about other choices. A hard shot does not automatically mean a free drop.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Your ball is in the dent it made when it landed after your last shot. Part is below ground level, not just below the tops of the grass.
Most of the course, including fairways and rough. It leaves out bunkers, penalty areas, and the starting area and green for the hole you are playing.
The part of a hole where the grass is usually cut short, between the starting area and the green.

questions.teachingTip: Show children what 'embedded' looks like and the difference between fairway and longer rough or sandy areas.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Yes, every ball stuck in sand gets a free drop.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Yes, only sand in a bunker stops a free drop.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Relief for Embedded Ball in Sand in the General Area
questions.question: Your ball is embedded in sand in rough in the general area that is not cut to fairway height or less. No Local Rule extends relief. Is free embedded-ball relief allowed?

choices.text: No. The ball is embedded in sand in an area not cut to fairway height or less.
Yes, free relief is always given for an embedded ball anywhere in the general area, including sand.
Yes, free relief is only not allowed if the ball is embedded in sand in a bunker.
No, relief is never given for an embedded ball in the general area.

questions.explanation: The usual embedded-ball permission excludes sand in parts of the general area not cut to fairway height or less. The question specifies that no Local Rule extends that permission.

questions.title: A ball stuck in a bunker or pond area
questions.question: A penalty area is often marked with red or yellow stakes or lines. Your ball sticks in its own dent in a bunker or a penalty area. Does being stuck there, by itself, give you a free drop?

choices.text: No.
Yes, stuck balls always get a free drop.
Yes in a penalty area, but not in a bunker.
Yes, if you say you cannot play the ball.

questions.explanation: No. Being stuck in its own dent does not give a free drop in either of those places. There may be a way to move it by adding penalty shots. The choices depend on which area the ball is in. Ask an adult to help.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A specially prepared area of sand. A grassy bank beside or inside its edge is not itself part of the bunker.
A water area, or another area the organisers name, with special rules for moving your ball. It is usually marked red or yellow. Sometimes you may play from it without a penalty.
Your ball is in the dent it made when it landed after your last shot. Part is below ground level, not just below the tops of the grass.

questions.teachingTip: Let children know that not all parts of the golf course have the same rules for a stuck ball. Show them the difference between the general area, bunkers, and penalty areas.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Yes, stuck balls always get a free drop.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Embedded Ball in a Bunker or Penalty Area
questions.question: Does a ball qualify for free embedded-ball relief under Rule 16.3 merely because it is embedded in a bunker or penalty area?

choices.text: No. Rule 16.3 does not give free embedded-ball relief in either area.
Yes, you always get embedded-ball relief anywhere on the course.
Yes, but only in penalty areas, not in bunkers.
Yes, but only if you declare the ball unplayable.

questions.explanation: Rule 16.3 is a general-area relief rule. This does not mean the ball must always be played as it lies: unplayable-ball relief can be available in a bunker under Rule 19.3, and penalty-area relief under Rule 17. Those options carry penalties.

questions.title: What does a ball stuck in its own dent look like?
questions.question: The rules call a ball stuck in its own dent an embedded ball. Your ball is on the fairway. Which description matches that meaning?

choices.text: It landed after your last shot, made its own dent, and is partly below ground level.
It is below ground level, however it got there.
It must be completely underground.
It is sitting in an old hole made by someone’s club.

questions.explanation: The ball must be in the dent made when it landed after your last shot. Part of it must be below ground level. Being hidden by tall grass does not count. Neither does sitting in an old hole or being pushed into the ground by a foot.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Your ball is in the dent it made when it landed after your last shot. Part is below ground level, not just below the tops of the grass.
Most of the course, including fairways and rough. It leaves out bunkers, penalty areas, and the starting area and green for the hole you are playing.
A piece of grass and soil dug up by a club. The hole left behind is a divot hole.

questions.teachingTip: Use a drawing or a spare ball in a practice area to compare ground level with the tops of the grass. Do not damage the course for a demonstration.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “It is below ground level, however it got there.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: When is a ball considered embedded?
questions.question: A ball is in the general area. Which description satisfies the embedded-ball test in Rule 16.3?

choices.text: It is partly below ground level in its own pitch-mark made when it landed after the player’s previous stroke.
Whenever it is below the surface of the ground, no matter how it got there.
Only when it is completely under the surface of the ground.
Whenever it is lying in a divot hole in the general area.

questions.explanation: The ball must be in its own pitch-mark from the previous stroke, with part below ground level. Grass height is not ground level. A ball pressed down by a foot, dropped into a dent, or driven straight into the ground without becoming airborne does not meet this test.

questions.title: A club broken when you were angry
questions.question: You hit your driver against the ground in anger and break it. May you fix it during this round?

choices.text: No.
Yes, because you need it.
Yes, if a referee agrees.
No, but you may bring in another club to replace it.

questions.explanation: No. The damaged-club rule does not allow repair or replacement after damage caused in anger. Use another club already allowed in your bag. Ask an adult to check the broken club. Do not use it if it could hurt someone.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A club often used for long shots from the tee.
The set of holes you are meant to play, in order. It may be 18 holes or fewer.

questions.teachingTip: Talk to young players about keeping calm on the course and taking care of their clubs, even if a shot goes badly.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Yes, because you need it.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Repairing Clubs Damaged Through Abuse
questions.question: If you damage your adjustable driver by slamming it on the ground in frustration, may you repair it during the round?

choices.text: No, you may not repair it during the round.
Yes, you may repair it because you need a functioning club.
Yes, but only if you obtain permission from a referee.
No, but you may bring in a replacement club from outside your playing set.

questions.explanation: Damage caused by abuse is excluded from the permission to repair or replace a club during the round under Rule 4.1a(2). The player may use other clubs already carried and may continue with the damaged club, but should not use equipment that is unsafe.

questions.title: A practice swing touches bunker sand
questions.question: You are playing match play, trying to win each hole. Your ball is in a bunker. Before hitting it, you make a practice swing that touches sand in that bunker. What is the penalty?

choices.text: You lose the hole.
No penalty.
Only a warning.
One penalty shot.

questions.explanation: You lose the hole. A practice swing must not touch sand in the bunker where your ball is, even by accident. This does not mean every touch of bunker sand is banned. For example, you may usually put spare clubs down without testing or improving the sand.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A specially prepared area of sand. A grassy bank beside or inside its edge is not itself part of the bunker.
A game in which you try to win holes against another player or team.
A swing to practise the movement. You are not trying to hit the ball.

questions.title: Practice swing touches sand in match play

The player must play the ball as it lies with no penalty.
The player receives a warning for the first offence.
The player receives a one stroke penalty.

questions.explanation: The general penalty is loss of hole in match play. Contact with sand during a practice swing in the bunker where the ball lies is prohibited even when the contact was accidental. Not every kind of contact with bunker sand is prohibited.

questions.title: Moving a ball from thick grass with a penalty
questions.question: Owen finds his ball in thick grass, outside bunkers and penalty areas. He decides to use the unplayable-ball rule rather than hit it there. Which answer describes his choices?

choices.text: Add one penalty shot and choose: play from the last place, drop back on a line, or drop within two club-lengths.
He must hit it from the thick grass.
He may move it anywhere for free.
He may move it for free only if another player agrees.

questions.explanation: Owen decides whether to use this rule. Each choice costs one penalty shot. He can play again from his last place. Or he can drop farther back on a line from the hole through his ball. Or he can drop within two club-lengths of the ball, no closer to the hole. Ask an adult to help find the allowed space.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: Outside a penalty area, you may decide not to hit the ball where it lies. This rule gives other choices with a penalty, even if a shot is possible.
One extra shot added to your score under a rule. You do not actually hit an extra shot to serve the penalty.
Let the ball fall straight down from the height of your knee when standing. Do not throw or spin it. It must reach the ground before touching you or your equipment.

questions.teachingTip: Let children see and practise the three options for an unplayable ball so they understand what to do in real games.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “He must hit it from the thick grass.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “He may move it anywhere for free.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “He may move it for free only if another player agrees.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: When can you declare your ball unplayable?
questions.question: Owen has found and identified his ball in thick grass in the general area and decides it is unplayable. Which relief options are available?

choices.text: Owen may take stroke and distance relief, back-on-the-line relief, or lateral relief, each for one penalty stroke.
Owen must play the ball as it lies; he has no relief options.
Owen may remove the ball from the thick grass without penalty.
Owen may only take free relief if another player agrees the ball is unplayable.

questions.explanation: Each Rule 19.2 option costs one penalty stroke: replay from the previous place; drop back on the line from the hole through the ball; or take lateral relief within two club-lengths of the ball, no nearer the hole. Each has its own dropping limits. Owen decides whether to use this rule.

questions.title: A ball on grass above a bunker
questions.question: Leah’s ball stops on a grassy bank above a bunker. It touches no sand and is outside all red or yellow penalty areas. Is her ball in the bunker?

choices.text: No. It is on the grassy bank outside the bunker.
Yes, because it is close to the sand.
Only if her feet are in the bunker.
Yes. Every grassy bank next to a bunker is part of it.

questions.explanation: No. This grassy bank is outside the bunker. Being close to the sand does not put her ball in it. Where her feet are does not change where the ball is. This matters when choosing the rules for a difficult shot.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A specially prepared area of sand. A grassy bank beside or inside its edge is not itself part of the bunker.
Most of the course, including fairways and rough. It leaves out bunkers, penalty areas, and the starting area and green for the hole you are playing.
Outside a penalty area, you may decide not to hit the ball where it lies. This rule gives other choices with a penalty, even if a shot is possible.

likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Yes, because it is close to the sand.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Ball in Grass Above a Bunker
questions.question: Leah’s ball rests on a grassy bank in the rough above a bunker. It touches no sand and is outside every penalty area. Is the ball in the bunker?

Yes, her ball is considered in the bunker because it is close to the sand.
Only if her stance is in the bunker, then it is considered in the bunker.
Yes, any bank surrounding a bunker is treated as part of the bunker.

questions.title: Going back after a shot into bushes
questions.question: Ben hits his ball into bushes beside the fairway. He decides to use the unplayable-ball rule. May he add one penalty shot and play again from the place where he hit his last shot?

choices.text: Yes.
No. He may only drop within two club-lengths of the ball.
No. He must hit it from the bushes.
Yes, but only if his last shot was from the tee.

Outside a penalty area, you may decide not to hit the ball where it lies. This rule gives other choices with a penalty, even if a shot is possible.
Most of the course, including fairways and rough. It leaves out bunkers, penalty areas, and the starting area and green for the hole you are playing.

questions.title: Taking Stroke and Distance Relief for an Unplayable Ball
questions.question: Ben’s ball has come to rest in thick bushes in the general area and he decides it is unplayable. May Ben take stroke and distance relief and play again from the spot where the previous stroke was made?

choices.text: Yes, he may take stroke and distance relief under one penalty stroke.
No, the only option is to take lateral relief two club-lengths from where the ball lies.
No, he must play the ball as it lies without penalty.
Yes, but only if the original stroke was played from the teeing area.

questions.explanation: Stroke-and-distance relief is available for one penalty stroke. The previous stroke still counts, and the next stroke also counts. Use Rule 14.6: teeing-area replay may be teed; a general-area replay normally uses a drop; a putting-green replay uses a placed ball.

questions.title: Picking up a glove moves your ball
questions.question: Isaac’s ball is on the fairway beside his glove, not in or on it. He picks up the glove and accidentally makes the ball move. What should he do?

choices.text: Put the ball back on its old spot, with no penalty.
Add one penalty shot and play from the new spot.
Add two penalty shots and put it back.
Play from the new spot, with no penalty.

questions.explanation: Isaac may pick up the glove. If doing that makes his ball move, there is no penalty, but he must put it back on its old spot. Estimate that spot carefully if needed. A loose glove is a movable object made by people.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: An object made by people that can be moved easily without damage, such as a bottle. Boundary markers and objects the course rules say must stay are different.

questions.teachingTip: Use a glove or bottle to show a movable obstruction. If removing it moves a ball resting beside it, put the ball back with no penalty. Compare a loose stick: on the fairway, moving the ball by removing that stick normally costs one penalty stroke.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Add one penalty shot and play from the new spot.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Add two penalty shots and put it back.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Play from the new spot, with no penalty.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Removing a Glove Lying Beside a Ball
questions.question: Isaac’s ball is at rest on the fairway beside, but not in or on, his glove. Removing the glove accidentally causes the ball to move. What is the ruling?

choices.text: There is no penalty. Isaac must replace the ball on its original spot, estimating that spot if necessary.
Isaac gets a one-stroke penalty and must play the ball as it lies.
Isaac gets a two-stroke penalty and must replace the ball.
There is no penalty and Isaac may play the ball from its new position.

questions.explanation: A glove lying on the ground is a movable obstruction, and it may be removed without penalty. If the ball moves while removing the movable obstruction, Rule 15.2a(1) states there is no penalty, but the ball must be replaced on its original spot, estimating the spot if necessary.

questions.title: A sprinkler blocks a putt from off the green
questions.question: Amelia wants to putt from the short grass beside the green. A fixed sprinkler head blocks the ball’s path. It does not touch her ball or block her feet or swing. Is she automatically allowed a free drop?

choices.text: No. Check whether a special course rule allows a drop in this situation.
Yes. A sprinkler in the ball’s path always gives a free drop.
Yes, but only if the ball and sprinkler are both on the green.
Yes, just being close to the ball and green is enough.

questions.explanation: No. From off the green, a sprinkler only blocking the ball’s path does not automatically give a free drop. Some courses use an extra rule that allows it in certain situations. Ask an adult or official whether that rule is being used and applies here.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The part of a watering system in the ground that sprays water onto the grass.
An extra rule the organisers use for their course or competition. It must be allowed by the Rules of Golf.
An allowed way to move or change your ball. It may be free or cost penalty shots.

questions.teachingTip: Remind players to ask a grown-up or referee about any club rules for sprinkler heads blocking their shot before they pick up or move their ball.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Yes. A sprinkler in the ball’s path always gives a free drop.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Yes, but only if the ball and sprinkler are both on the green.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Yes, just being close to the ball and green is enough.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Sprinkler Head on the Line of Play – Off the Green
questions.question: Amelia’s ball is in the general area just off the green. A sprinkler head affects only her line of play, not her stance, swing or ball. Does she automatically get free relief?

choices.text: No, free relief is not automatic. She must check that an applicable Local Rule is in force and she meets its conditions.
Yes, Rule 16.1 always gives free relief from a sprinkler head if it interferes with the line of play.
Yes, but only if her ball and the sprinkler head are both on the putting green.
Yes, as long as the sprinkler head is within two club-lengths of both the ball and the green.

questions.explanation: Rule 16.1 does not grant relief for line-only interference when the ball is in the general area. Check whether a Local Rule for immovable obstructions close to the green is in force and whether all its conditions are met. Distance alone does not establish entitlement.

sceneSpec.educationalFocus: Clarifies accidental movement during a search and the requirement to replace the ball

questions.title: You nudge your ball while looking for it
questions.question: Oliver is looking for his ball in long grass. He accidentally nudges it with his shoe. The grass and ground where it was resting have not changed. What should he do?

choices.text: Put the ball back on its old spot, with no penalty.
Add one penalty shot and play from the new spot.
Add two penalty shots and put it back.
Play from the new spot, with no penalty.

questions.explanation: There is no penalty for accidentally moving the ball while looking for it. Oliver must put it back on its old spot. If he does not know the exact spot, he should make a careful estimate using what he saw.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A rule may add extra shots to your score or make you lose a hole. Some penalties mean your result cannot count in the competition.
Put the ball down by hand on the required spot and let go. If it will not stay there, follow the extra steps in the rules.

questions.teachingTip: You can remind children to be careful while searching for their ball, but not to worry if they accidentally move it – just put it back!
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Add one penalty shot and play from the new spot.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Add two penalty shots and put it back.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Play from the new spot, with no penalty.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Moving a Ball During a Search
questions.question: While searching in long grass, Oliver accidentally nudges his ball with his shoe. The original lie is not altered. What must he do?

choices.text: No penalty. Replace the ball on its original spot, estimating it if necessary.
Oliver gets a one-stroke penalty and must play the ball from its new position.
Oliver gets a two-stroke penalty and must return the ball to its original spot.
There is no penalty and the ball may be played from where it was moved to.

questions.explanation: There is no penalty for accidental movement during search. Replace the ball on its original spot; if that spot is unknown, estimate it. The scenario states that the lie was not altered.

questions.title: You kick your ball before looking for it
questions.question: Hannah is walking towards the rough where she thinks her ball went. She has not started looking for it and is not taking an allowed drop. She accidentally kicks her own ball. What should she do?

choices.text: Add one penalty shot and put the ball back.
Put it back, with no penalty.
Play from the new spot, with no penalty.
Add two penalty shots and play from the new spot.

questions.explanation: Hannah gets one penalty shot and must put the ball back on its old spot. Estimate that spot carefully if needed. She had not started looking for the ball, so the special no-penalty rule for moving it during a search does not apply.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A rule may add extra shots to your score or make you lose a hole. Some penalties mean your result cannot count in the competition.
Put the ball down by hand on the required spot and let go. If it will not stay there, follow the extra steps in the rules.
The longer grass beside the fairway.

questions.teachingTip: Describe how to be careful not to move your ball when you are close to it, even before you start looking for it.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Put it back, with no penalty.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Play from the new spot, with no penalty.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Add two penalty shots and play from the new spot.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Penalty for Moving Ball Before Starting Search
questions.question: Hannah is walking through rough towards where she expects her ball to be. She has not started looking for or identifying it and is not applying a relief rule. She accidentally kicks her own ball. What is the ruling?

choices.text: Hannah receives one penalty stroke and must replace the ball.
There is no penalty, but the ball must be replaced.
Hannah must play the ball as it lies from its new position without penalty.
Hannah receives a two-stroke penalty but must play the ball as it lies.

questions.explanation: The no-penalty search exception does not apply because Hannah had not started searching or identifying her ball. Add one penalty stroke and replace the ball on its original spot, estimating that spot if necessary.

Two junior golfers studying the balls closely but unsure
Fairway visible in the background

questions.title: Two balls look exactly the same
questions.question: Samuel and Grace find two identical balls in the rough. They cannot tell which ball belongs to whom, and their time to search and check is over. Neither played a spare ball. No special course rule gives another choice. What must they do?

choices.text: Each adds one penalty shot and plays again from their last place.
Choose one ball each and carry on.
Take the ball nearest the direction each shot went.
Agree to start the hole again, with no penalty.

questions.explanation: Both balls count as lost because neither player can identify their own in time. Each player counts the last shot, adds one penalty shot and plays again from their previous place. They must count the next shot too. Putting a personal mark on a ball before playing helps avoid this problem.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: One extra shot added to your score under a rule. You do not actually hit an extra shot to serve the penalty.
Add one penalty shot and play again from your last shot’s place. Count that earlier shot too. How you restart depends on where you hit from.
A ball you have checked is yours, for example by finding your own mark on it.

questions.teachingTip: Before playing, put an identification mark on your ball. Practise checking the mark carefully rather than guessing which ball is yours.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Choose one ball each and carry on.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Take the ball nearest the direction each shot went.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Agree to start the hole again, with no penalty.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Two balls are found but cannot be identified
questions.question: Samuel and Grace find two identical balls in the rough. Neither can identify their own ball after the allowed search and identification time has ended. Neither has played a provisional and no alternative Local Rule applies. What must they do?

choices.text: Both balls are treated as lost. Each player must take stroke and distance relief: add one penalty stroke and play again from where their previous stroke was made.
Samuel and Grace can agree to each take one ball and continue playing with it.
The nearest ball to each player’s line of play is assumed to belong to that player.
If both players agree, they may replay the hole without penalty.

questions.explanation: If two balls are found but neither player can identify which ball is theirs, both balls are treated as lost. Each player must take stroke and distance relief, which means adding one penalty stroke and returning to play from where the previous stroke was made. The players cannot simply select a ball each or make assumptions based on which lies where. (Rules 7.2, 18.2a(1), 18.2b, 14.6)

questions.title: Brushing sand off the green
questions.question: Amelia wants to putt from just outside the green. There is sand on the green between her ball and the hole. May she brush that sand off the green before playing?

choices.text: Yes, even though her ball is off the green.
No. Her ball must be on the green first.
No. Sand must never be removed.
Yes, but only with her hand, not a club.

questions.explanation: Yes. Sand and loose soil may be removed from the green before a shot. Her ball does not have to be on the green. This special permission is for sand on the green, not sand on the short grass beside it.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The area around the hole prepared for putting. It may be flat or sloping.
A forward swing made to hit the ball. If you try to hit it but miss, that still counts as a shot.

questions.teachingTip: Before a shot, show how to gently remove sand from the putting green. This permission does not extend to brushing sand away from the fringe.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “No. Her ball must be on the green first.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “No. Sand must never be removed.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Yes, but only with her hand, not a club.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Removing sand from the putting green
questions.question: Amelia’s ball is off the green, but she wants to putt. There is sand on the putting green between her ball and the hole. Can she remove the sand from the green before playing her stroke?

choices.text: Yes, she may remove sand from the putting green, whether or not her ball is on that green.
No, she may only remove sand if her ball is on the green.
No, sand may not be removed under any circumstance.
Yes, but only if she uses her hand and not a club.

questions.explanation: Rule 13.1c(1) allows sand and loose soil to be removed from the putting green without penalty, whether the player's ball is on or off the green. The permission specifically relates to sand on the putting green, not the fringe or any other area.

questions.title: Permission to pick up another player’s ball
questions.question: Elise and Adrian are counting all their shots in individual stroke play. Elise is another player, not Adrian’s helper or teammate. Adrian says she may lift his ball on the green all round. Does she still need his permission each time?

No, once covers the whole round.
Only a referee may lift another player’s ball.
No, if she is keeping his score.

questions.explanation: Yes. Permission for the whole round is not enough. Adrian must give permission for each time Elise lifts his ball. She should mark its spot before lifting it. A caddie, the player’s own helper during the round, has different permissions.

questions.teachingTip: For another competitor such as Elise, practise getting permission for each lifting. Explain that a caddie or team partner has different permissions.

questions.title: Permission to Mark and Lift Another Player’s Ball
questions.question: In individual stroke play, Elise is another competitor, not Adrian’s caddie. Adrian tells her she may lift his ball on the putting green whenever needed for the whole round. Must she get fresh authorisation for a later lifting?

No. One authorisation covers every lifting for the rest of the round.
No one except a referee may lift another player’s ball.
Acting as the score marker automatically authorises every lifting.

questions.explanation: An authorised helper such as Elise needs authorisation for each lifting. It need not be phrased as a particular question, but general permission for the whole round is insufficient. A caddie has separate permissions; Elise is explicitly not the caddie.

questions.title: Picking up someone else’s ball without asking
questions.question: You are counting all your shots in individual stroke play. You are not the other player’s helper or teammate. You pick up their ball on the green without permission or marking its spot. What must happen?

choices.text: No one gets a penalty. Put the ball back on its old spot.
You get one penalty shot.
The other player gets one penalty shot.
Both of you get one penalty shot.

questions.explanation: Neither player gets a penalty in this situation. The ball must go back on its old spot. You or the player may put it back; estimate the spot carefully if needed. Ask before touching someone else’s ball. In match play, picking up another player’s ball can have a different penalty.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The area around the hole prepared for putting. It may be flat or sloping.
A small object made by people, such as a coin or tee. Put it right beside or behind your ball to show its spot.
One extra shot added to your score under a rule. You do not actually hit an extra shot to serve the penalty.

questions.teachingTip: Ask before touching another player’s ball. Practise marking a spot before an authorised lift, then returning the ball accurately.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “You get one penalty shot.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “The other player gets one penalty shot.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Both of you get one penalty shot.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Lifting another player’s ball without permission in stroke play
questions.question: In individual stroke play, you lift another competitor’s ball from the putting green without authorisation and without marking its spot. You are not their caddie. What is the ruling?

choices.text: There is no penalty to either player, and the ball must be replaced on its original spot.
The player who lifted the ball gets one penalty stroke.
The owner of the ball receives one penalty stroke.
Both players receive a penalty of one stroke.

questions.explanation: Neither player is penalised when a competitor's ball is lifted by another player without permission in stroke play. The ball must be replaced on its original spot by either player, using estimation if necessary. This follows Rule 9.6 and relevant procedures for replacing a ball moved by an outside influence.

questions.title: Picking up your opponent’s ball
questions.question: Lewis and Ava are playing match play, trying to win each hole. Lewis knows which ball is Ava’s. He picks it up from the fairway without asking. He is not helping with a search, giving her the next shot, or following another rule. What happens?

choices.text: Lewis adds one penalty shot. Ava gets no penalty; her ball must go back.
Ava adds one penalty shot.
Nobody gets a penalty; put the ball back.
Lewis loses the hole.

questions.explanation: Lewis gets one penalty shot for lifting Ava’s ball without permission here. Ava gets none. Put her ball back on its old spot, estimating that spot carefully if needed. Trying to help does not automatically give Lewis permission to pick it up.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A game in which you try to win holes against another player or team.
One extra shot added to your score under a rule. You do not actually hit an extra shot to serve the penalty.
Most of the course, including fairways and rough. It leaves out bunkers, penalty areas, and the starting area and green for the hole you are playing.

questions.teachingTip: Remind children to always ask their friend before picking up someone else’s ball, even if they are trying to help.

questions.title: Lifting an Opponent’s Ball Without Permission in Match Play
questions.question: In individual match play, Lewis deliberately lifts Ava’s identified ball from the general area without permission. Nobody is searching for or identifying the ball, and he is not conceding a stroke or applying another Rule. What is the ruling?

choices.text: Lewis receives one penalty stroke; Ava receives no penalty, and her ball must be replaced on its original spot.
Ava receives one penalty stroke because her ball was lifted.
Neither player receives a penalty, but play must continue from where the ball was lifted.
Lewis loses the hole.

questions.explanation: Lewis gets one penalty stroke and Ava gets none. Replace Ava’s ball on its original spot, estimating it if necessary. The facts exclude the exceptions for search, mistaken identification on the green, permission and concession.

questions.title: Two mistakes on the green
questions.question: You are playing match play, trying to win each hole. On the green, you accidentally move the other player’s ball-marker. Later, you mark and pick up their ball because you think it is yours. What must happen?

choices.text: No penalty for either mistake. Put the marker and ball back in their old places.
Add one penalty shot for each mistake.
You lose the hole for picking up their ball.
No penalty for the marker, but one penalty shot for lifting the ball.

questions.explanation: Neither mistake gets a penalty here. Restore the marker to show the original spot. Put the ball you lifted by mistake back on its own original spot. If you do not know a spot exactly, estimate it carefully. These permissions apply to the stated mistakes on the green.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A small object made by people, such as a coin or tee. Put it right beside or behind your ball to show its spot.
The area around the hole prepared for putting. It may be flat or sloping.

questions.teachingTip: Remind children to look closely at which ball and marker they are using, and to say "sorry" if they move someone else’s marker or ball by accident.

questions.title: Accidental Movement and Mistaken Ball on the Green
questions.question: In two separate incidents on the putting green in match play, you accidentally move your opponent’s ball-marker, then later correctly mark and lift their ball believing it is your own. What is the ruling?

choices.text: No penalty in either incident. Restore the original marked spot and replace the lifted ball on its original spot.
You get one penalty stroke for moving the ball-marker and another for lifting the ball.
You lose the hole for lifting your opponent’s ball without permission.
There is no penalty for moving the marker, but you get one penalty stroke for lifting the ball.

questions.explanation: Accidental movement of a ball-marker on the putting green is not penalised. Marking and lifting an opponent’s ball there in the mistaken belief it is your own is also exempt. Restore the marker or ball to the required original spot, estimating a spot if necessary.

questions.title: Who may put Jack’s ball back?
questions.question: Jack is playing an individual stroke-play competition, counting all his shots. He marks and lifts his ball on the green. Nobody else lifted or moved it. Who may put it back?

choices.text: Jack.
Anyone in his group.
Only the person keeping Jack’s score.
Jack’s helper may always do it, even though they did not lift or move it.

questions.explanation: Jack may put it back. The usual rule allows the player or the person who lifted or moved the ball to do that. Here, Jack was the only person who lifted or moved it. Keeping his score or being his helper does not automatically give someone else permission.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The area around the hole prepared for putting. It may be flat or sloping.
A small object made by people, such as a coin or tee. Put it right beside or behind your ball to show its spot.

questions.teachingTip: Let kids practise marking, lifting, and replacing their ball on the green so they learn who is allowed to put the ball back.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Anyone in his group.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Only the person keeping Jack’s score.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Jack’s helper may always do it, even though they did not lift or move it.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: Who is allowed to replace a ball that has been marked and lifted?
questions.question: In individual stroke play, Jack marks and lifts his own ball on the putting green. No one else has lifted or moved it. Who may replace it under the usual replacement rule?

choices.text: Jack may replace it himself.
Anyone playing in the group may replace it.
Only the player keeping Jack’s score may replace it.
Jack’s caddie may always replace the ball, even if the caddie did not lift or move the ball.

questions.explanation: Under the usual Rule 14.2b(1), the player or a person who lifted or caused the ball to move may replace it. Jack himself lifted it in this scenario, so Jack is eligible. Being a caddie or score marker alone does not grant permission to replace it.

questions.title: The wrong person puts a ball back
questions.question: Theo is counting all his shots in an individual stroke-play competition. He marks and lifts his ball on the green. Another player, Emma, puts it back on the right spot with his permission. She had not lifted or moved it. How can Theo fix this?

choices.text: Before hitting it, lift it and put it back himself, with no penalty.
Do nothing. His permission makes Emma’s action allowed.
Leave the competition immediately.
Add one penalty shot to Emma’s score.

questions.explanation: Theo should lift the ball and put it back himself before hitting it. Then there is no penalty for this mistake. His permission alone did not allow Emma to put it back. If he plays from the right spot without fixing who put it there, he gets one penalty shot.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: The area around the hole prepared for putting. It may be flat or sloping.
Your helper during a round. They may carry your clubs and give advice about your shots.
One extra shot added to your score under a rule. You do not actually hit an extra shot to serve the penalty.

questions.teachingTip: Use a spare ball to practise who lifted it and who can put it back. Explain that fixing this before hitting avoids the penalty.
likelyMisconceptions: If the learner chooses “Do nothing. His permission makes Emma’s action allowed.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Leave the competition immediately.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.
If the learner chooses “Add one penalty shot to Emma’s score.”, ask them to explain their choice. Compare it with the stated facts and explanation.

questions.title: A person who is not eligible replaces the ball
questions.question: In individual stroke play, Theo marks and lifts his own ball on the green. Emma did not lift or move it, but replaces it on the correct spot with Theo’s permission. The usual replacement rule applies. How can Theo correct this?

choices.text: Before playing, Theo can lift and correctly replace it himself without penalty. If he plays it without correcting the unauthorised replacement, he gets one penalty stroke.
No penalty applies as Theo gave Emma permission to replace the ball.
Theo is disqualified for a serious breach of the Rules.
Emma gets a penalty stroke, but Theo does not.

questions.explanation: Theo’s permission alone does not make Emma eligible to replace the ball. Theo can correct the procedure under Rule 14.5 before playing. If he plays from the correct spot without correcting who replaced it, the penalty is one stroke.
